text: Hi, everyone.

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: My name is Paula, and I am one of the engineers on the Toland team, specifically focusing on our iOS app.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And for the next 20 minutes or so, I'll be talking about what it takes to build a voice-first AI companion and also about how we use AI to build AI internally.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So humanity has always imagined the perfect companion.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And these are all different stories, but they exhibit the same longing for something that listens, remembers you, and is wholly specifically yours.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Okay, so people talk to Toland a lot.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We support both text and voice chat, but we have over four million hours of voice conversation so far.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We say Toland is a voice-first companion even though we support both because it's the voice experience that's truly immersive and that makes users' relationships with their Tolands feel real.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But the moment this relationship is a spoken relationship, the engineering problem changes completely.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So let me show you how voice breaks the normal way we build and interact with LLMs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the core difference really is that in a text chatbot, turns are relatively slow and context is stable.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The user waits a few seconds, they read, and they tend to stay on topic.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And almost every LLM app assumes that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Voice is the opposite.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Turns are fast.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Your whole round trip from the user finishing their sentence to the Toland starting to speak has to land in under a couple of seconds, or it stops feeling like a conversation.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the context is volatile.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: People talk to their Tolands while they're cooking, while they're walking, while they're falling asleep.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They change their subjects mid-sentence.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They say, um, they interrupt.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that two seconds is crucial.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Early on, our latency drifted from two seconds to about two and a half seconds, and that half second tanked basically every metric in the product.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: People would write in to complain that their tolerance were too slow.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And living inside this constraint has taught us a lot and gave us four principles.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Principle one is that you have to design for conversational volatility.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Again, text users stay on topic, but voice users jump around.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Someone could be mid-story about their breakup and suddenly go, wait, did I leave the stove on?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then back.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Speech is messy.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Most LLM apps assume that you'll have a clean and stable conversation, and we had to build for the opposite.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So for a long time, that meant fixing things that sound tiny but are actually the product.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So you can't interrupt a toll in mid-sentence.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A short yes or yeah won't register as a turn.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For example, curse words will get stripped out.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the deeper lesson was to stop optimizing for fewer interruptions and start optimizing for fewer bad ones where the agent would jump in way too early.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we built smart turn-taking that reads your speech pattern to decide whether an interruption is real, and we cut the worst early aborts by more than half.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we happily paid about 60 milliseconds of extra latency to do it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Principle two.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Latency isn't just a number you check at the end, it's actually the product, and we measure every stage of the pipeline separately because it feels slow is useless.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You have to know where exactly it's slow.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the pipeline here is that the user stops talking, we detect end of utterance, we transcribe, and then the model produces its first token.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So time to first token, often the biggest chunk, is around a second.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The model finishes generating, and then text to speech produces its first byte, and then it plays back to the user.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A couple lessons here.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So one, so far, our biggest jump in quality came from moving to GPT 5.1 on the responses API, which cut our time to speech by more than 7 tenths of a second, which is huge.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Two, we don't send every turn to the same model.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We run a tiered fleet.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we use a frontier model for the turns that carry the relationship with your tollen.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So for example, your first conversation with your tollen and your onboarding.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we use smaller and faster models for the lightweight turns.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the whole game then becomes about routing or deciding turn by turn which model you actually need.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we run a small classifier we call the Tone Router on every single turn.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this Tone Router itself runs on a cheap model.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it reads the emotional state of the conversation.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And our main principle is that we route based on stakes, not on cost.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the high-stakes moments always get the best model.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this would be, again, the user's very first message, their first few days of their toll, and anything that we deem to be emotionally serious.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For example, we have crisis or therapist-style tones, and we never cheap out on those.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then the lighter, casual back and forth can ride on smaller models that are faster and cheaper.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And all the background work, so that's summarizing the conversation, generating personas, the tone router itself run on these small models too.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And why would we go to all this trouble?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's mainly because the frontier model costs us roughly five times the smaller one.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So one big model turn is about five smaller model turns.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So routing is a huge part of what makes the unit economics for us actually work.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we do a bunch of A-B experiments, and the surprising result we found there is that routing a third of our turns to the small model has almost no measurable effect on retention.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And principle three is what makes a companion feel like a companion.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the naive approach is to keep the whole conversation history as a sort of transcript, but that doesn't fit into our two-second loop.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It doesn't scale, and it just doesn't work.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It leads to long sessions degrading.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It leads to the model getting lost in the middle of a huge context and also hallucinating.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So instead, we see memory as a sort of retrieval system.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We pull facts, preferences, and emotional vibe signals out of conversations.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We embed them and we store them in a vector database with sub-50 millisecond lookups.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And every night, we compress.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we merge duplicates, we cluster related memories, we resolve contradictions, and we drop all the noise.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we don't just retrieve against users' last messages, we also generate internal questions about the person and their relationship and retrieve against those.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So, and we also split memory into two parts.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We have stable memory and unstable memory.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The volatile stuff lives in the live tail of the prompt, and when we summarize a conversation, we look at which memories actually get recalled and pin those into a stable and cacheable block.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The last principle is around context.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Specifically, you should rebuild context and not fight drift.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So most apps reuse context across turns to keep the cache warm.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And in a stable text chat, that's fine.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But in a volatile voice conversation, it's a trap because the second the user pivots, your reuse context is actively wrong.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So every turn, we reassemble the context window from parts.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We have a summary of recent messages.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We have the user's persona card, the memories we just retrieved, tone guidance from the emotional signal, and real-time app state.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And what also really helps us in the case of Tolan is that our characters aren't generic or assistants with no personality.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Everyone is crafted, and we in fact have an in-house science fiction novelist, Eliot, who writes the Tolan character lore.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And a couple of interesting points here.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So one, why did we go with an alien?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Mostly because there's no real-world reference to anchor on, which means that users can project onto it, and it becomes what they need.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The baseline tollen is bubbly, it's youthful, it's irreverent, and also if an alien character acts a bit unpredictably, so if it's impulsive or chaotic or otherwise violates the norms the user would expect, it's not particularly surprising.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you look at aliens in TV shows or in plays, there's a lot of humorous moments around this, and this kind of chaos reads as charming.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Second, we also know that personality is worthless if it drifts.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So yeah, we run this parallel tone monitoring system that changes how a line is delivered based on your emotional cues without changing who the character is, holding identity across hundreds of turns.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And since we're at an AI conference, I thought I would also spend a bit of time talking about how we not just ship AI, but also use AI to build it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I'm sure this is the case for most of you in the room now, but basically as of late last year, Claude has co-authored more code in our iOS app than any individual engineer in the team.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I think especially a few months ago, everyone's instinct was to be kind of suspicious because more AI code meant more slop.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But our crash-free rate actually went from 99.6% to 99.9%.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Runtime errors dropped by over 50%.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And our share of highly engaged users doubled.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the biggest lesson in building that system is that an agent's context comes mostly from the code base itself, not so much from the Cloud MD file.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We found that it's far more powerful to make the code base be the documentation, so we had agents standardize it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: On top of that, we run a real fleet of agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We have implementation agents that think freely and just get us to work in code.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They build it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They check it against snapshots until it's pixel perfect.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then we have separate review agents that enforce our standards.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So multiple Claude's basically review each other before a human looks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then we have a PR shepherd that watches an open pull request and keeps iterating against CI failures and review comments until it's clean.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we also have a triage bot that fires on every inbound bug report that we get, and they're all wired through MCP into linear, into Sentry, Datadog, so an agent can reconstruct a crash and route it itself and oftentimes open the PR on its own and just fix the bug.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we also, we ship on evals.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So for example, we've been working on a new character targeted towards an older demographic.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And Elliot, our in-house novelist, basically built this entire new character in a day.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the agents mapped every personality-bearing surface in the code.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They wrote a sort of a voice bible.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then they had five judges attack it from different angles.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Archetype fidelity, the model mechanics, our code standards, the ears of a skeptical 52-year-old, and safety.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then they evaluated the changes against real production logs over three find, fix, verify rounds.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And over seven million tokens and four and a half hours of compute later, he ended up with basically a couple of weeks of work done in an afternoon.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And does this work?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Well, I'll let the users tell you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We're at 4.8 stars on the App Store across 162,000 reviews.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And when we survey users on well-being, the highest scoring dimension by far is emotional safety.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is definitely a bar that being voice first sets.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So when the interface is your voice and the thing on the other side remembers you and has a personality, it stops being just software and starts being an actual relationship, which is why building it responsibly and building it well is worth obsessing over.
